items.q: While the players (A) are warming up on the pitch yesterday evening, a sudden storm (B) forced the referee (C) to delay the match (D) by half an hour.
items.explanation: Yesterday evening places the action in the past, so the background action needs the past continuous: were warming up, not the present continuous.

items.q: Each of the paintings in the new gallery (A) on Le Loi Street (B) were painted by a young artist (C) who studied (D) in Hue.
options: were painted by a young artist
items.correction: was painted by a young artist
items.explanation: The subject is each, which is always singular; the plural noun after of does not change that, so the verb must be was painted.

items.q: The Mekong River, (A) which flows through six different countries (B) before reaching the sea, (C) is longest river (D) in Southeast Asia.
options: which flows through six different countries
items.explanation: A superlative adjective before a noun takes the definite article: the longest river.

items.q: The students (A) were told to hand in their essays (B) by Friday, but (C) several of them (D) arrived to school late and missed the deadline.
options: were told to hand in their essays
items.explanation: Arrive is followed by at (a building or small place) or in (a city or country), never by to.

items.q: Thanks to the (A) improve public transport, fewer people in the city centre (B) drive to work, and the air (C) has become (D) noticeably cleaner.
items.explanation: A word describing the noun transport must be an adjective; the past participle improved does that job, while improve is only a verb.

items.q: My aunt, (A) who lives in Can Tho, sent (B) my sister and I a box of mangoes (C) from her garden (D) last week.
items.explanation: The people receiving the mangoes are the object of sent, so the object pronoun me is needed; test it by dropping my sister and: sent me, not sent I.

items.q: The second half of the film was (A) far more exciting than the first, (B) although the ending was (C) more worse than (D) I had expected.
items.explanation: Worse is already the comparative of bad, so it cannot be combined with more; you could say much worse than or even worse than.

items.q: Children in remote villages (A) would have the same opportunities (B) as those in cities (C) if the government (D) will invest more money in rural schools.
items.explanation: Would have in the main clause signals a second conditional, whose if-clause takes the past simple: if the government invested. A future form such as will does not belong in the if-clause of a conditional.

items.q: The doctor asked my father (A) how long had he been feeling dizzy and (B) whether he (C) had taken any medicine (D) before coming to the clinic.
options: how long had he been feeling
items.correction: how long he had been feeling
items.explanation: In a reported question the subject comes before the verb, with no inversion: how long he had been feeling.

items.q: The old fisherman (A) who taught me to tie knots lives in a small house (B) which windows face the sea, (C) and he still (D) sails every morning.
options: who taught me to tie knots
items.explanation: The windows belong to the house, so the relative clause needs the possessive relative whose; which cannot show possession.

items.q: Nobody in the class (A) could explain (B) why the experiment failed, so the teacher asked (C) what had we done (D) with the samples.
items.explanation: After asked the question becomes an indirect one, so the subject goes before the auxiliary: what we had done.

items.q: Before the exam, our teacher (A) reminded us to (B) read the questions carefully and (C) not to waste time (D) doing careless mistakes.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is make a mistake; do does not combine with mistake.

items.q: There were (A) too much people at the market this morning, (B) so we (C) had to wait almost an hour (D) before anyone served us.
options: had to wait almost an hour
items.explanation: People is a plural countable noun, so it takes many; much is used only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: The old bridge was closed for repairs, (A) so the villagers had to cross the river by boat (B) despite it was raining heavily (C) for most of (D) the week.
options: so the villagers had to cross the river by boat
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form; a full clause with a subject and verb needs the conjunction although or even though.

items.q: By the time the fire engines (A) reached the warehouse, the flames (B) had spread to the roof and most of the goods inside (C) are already destroyed (D) beyond repair.
items.explanation: The destruction happened before the past moment marked by by the time the fire engines reached, so it needs the past perfect passive, not the present tense.

items.q: Physics, (A) which many students find (B) the most difficult subject, (C) becomes much easier when the teacher (D) use practical experiments instead of long lectures.
items.explanation: The teacher is a singular subject, so the present simple verb needs the -s ending: uses.

items.q: My father works as (A) engineer for a company (B) that builds wind turbines (C) along the coast (D) of Ninh Thuan province.
items.explanation: A singular countable job title needs an article, and because engineer begins with a vowel sound it takes an.

items.q: The museum, which (A) opened in 1998, is famous (B) with its collection of ancient pottery (C) discovered in the central highlands (D) during the 1970s.
items.explanation: The adjective famous is followed by for when we name the thing a place is known for.

items.q: Although the recipe (A) looked simple, my first attempt at baking bread (B) was a (C) completely disaster because I (D) forgot to add the yeast.
items.explanation: A word that describes the noun disaster must be an adjective (complete); the adverb completely can only modify a verb or adjective.

items.q: The city council (A) has promised to plant a thousand trees (B) along the main roads, but (C) so far it (D) has planted only a few of it.
options: has planted only a few of it
items.correction: has planted only a few of them
items.explanation: The pronoun refers back to a thousand trees, a plural noun, so it must be them; it can only stand for a singular noun.

items.q: Learning to swim is (A) much more easier than most adults think, (B) provided that the learner (C) practises regularly (D) with a patient instructor.
items.explanation: Easy is a short adjective whose comparative is formed with -er, so more must not be added: much easier.

items.q: If you (A) mix yellow and blue paint together, you (B) would get green, (C) which is why (D) children learn this rule first in art class.
options: mix yellow and blue paint together
items.explanation: This is a general truth, a zero conditional, so both clauses take the present simple: if you mix …, you get. Would belongs to an imaginary second conditional.

items.q: Minh's mother asked him (A) whether he had finished his homework, and he (B) replied that he (C) will do it after dinner (D) that evening.
options: whether he had finished his homework
items.explanation: The reporting verb replied is in the past, so will in the original words shifts back to would in reported speech.

items.q: Sapa, (A) where thousands of tourists go every winter, is (B) one of the few places in Vietnam (C) in which snow sometimes falls, (D) that surprises many foreign visitors.
options: where thousands of tourists go every winter
one of the few places in Vietnam
items.explanation: A relative clause that comments on the whole previous statement is non-defining, follows a comma and must begin with which; that is never used after a comma.

items.q: My cousin (A) isn't enough old to ride a motorbike, so every morning her father (B) drives her to school (C) before he goes (D) to the office.
items.explanation: Enough comes after an adjective (old enough) but before a noun (enough money).

items.q: During the school trip to Hoi An, my classmates (A) bought silk lanterns, (B) made hundreds of photos and (C) tried (D) every street snack they could find.
options: every street snack they could find
items.explanation: In English you take a photo; make a photo is not a natural collocation.

items.q: Although (A) there is (B) plenty of information on the internet, (C) a few of it is reliable, so students (D) must check their sources carefully.
options: a few of it is reliable
items.explanation: Information is uncountable, so the quantifier must be little; a few is only used with plural countable nouns.

items.q: The match (A) was cancelled at the last minute, (B) and hundreds of fans (C) went home disappointed (D) because of the pitch was flooded.
options: was cancelled at the last minute
because of the pitch was flooded
items.explanation: Because of is followed by a noun phrase, but here a full clause with subject and verb follows, so the conjunction because is needed.

items.q: I (A) know my best friend since we were in kindergarten, and we (B) have never had (C) a serious argument (D) in all those years.
items.explanation: Since marks a period that started in the past and continues now, which calls for the present perfect: have known.

items.q: Some of the new laptops (A) donated by a local company (B) is already broken, (C) even though the computer room (D) opened only last month.
items.explanation: With some of the verb agrees with the noun after of; laptops is plural, so the verb must be are.

items.q: During the summer holiday, my family (A) usually goes to (B) the beach on Sundays, and (C) the lunch is always (D) a picnic under the trees.
items.explanation: Names of meals used in a general sense (lunch, dinner, breakfast) take no article unless a particular meal is described.

items.q: The documentary (A) explains how penguins (B) survive the freezing winter (C) by huddling together (D) in the coast of Antarctica.
items.explanation: A coast is a line where land meets sea, so things are located on the coast, not in it.

items.q: The (A) scientific who discovered the vaccine (B) refused to accept any money (C) for her work, saying that (D) saving lives was reward enough.
items.explanation: After the and before who a noun for a person is needed: scientist. Scientific is an adjective.

items.q: Ha and Mai (A) finished the race at exactly the same time, so the judges (B) gave they both a gold medal (C) rather than choosing (D) a single winner.
options: finished the race at exactly the same time
gave they both a gold medal
items.correction: gave them both a gold medal
items.explanation: The girls receive the medal, so they are the object of gave and need the object pronoun them, not the subject pronoun they.

items.q: Of all the desserts, the coconut ice cream (A) was the cheapest, (B) but it turned out to be (C) the more delicious than the chocolate cake (D) we ordered.
options: but it turned out to be
items.explanation: A comparison with than uses the comparative form without the: more delicious than. The belongs with superlatives such as the cheapest.

items.q: If the driver (A) had noticed the warning sign, he (B) would have slowed down and the accident (C) at the crossroads (D) would never happen.
items.explanation: The sentence is a third conditional about an unreal past, so every result verb takes would have + past participle, matching would have slowed down.

items.q: The manager (A) said us that the shop would close early on the holiday (B) and asked (C) whether we could (D) finish stocking the shelves by noon.
options: finish stocking the shelves by noon
items.explanation: Tell takes a direct object for the listener (told us), whereas say needs to before the listener (said to us).

items.q: The library (A) has a quiet room on the top floor (B) where students can borrow for group projects (C) if they (D) book it a day in advance.
options: has a quiet room on the top floor
where students can borrow for group projects
book it a day in advance
items.correction: which students can borrow for group projects
items.explanation: The room is the thing being borrowed, the object of borrow, so the relative pronoun must be which or that; where only replaces an adverb of place.

items.q: My grandfather, who is eighty, (A) still enjoys walking (B) in the park, and he (C) always is the first person (D) to arrive there each morning.
items.explanation: Adverbs of frequency go after the verb be: he is always, although they go before other main verbs.

items.q: The team (A) trained hard all season, and their efforts (B) finally paid off when they (C) won the regional championship and (D) beat a new record.
items.explanation: A new record is one you set; you can only break or beat a record that already exists. Beat a new record mixes the two ideas and is not English.
